query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating that incorporates a graded interfacial layer enriched with adhesion‐promoting elements (such as Cr or Ti) will bond more effectively to a copper substrate while preserving the HEA’s inherent wear resistance when compared to a standard HEA coating directly deposited on Cu.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper (Cu) matrix with a clean, untreated surface.
generation.intervention: Deposit an HEA coating designed with a graded interfacial layer that transitions in composition from Cu to the bulk HEA—by introducing adhesion‐promoting elements (e.g., Cr or Ti) via a technique like magnetron sputtering, followed by controlled thermal treatment.
generation.conditions: Service conditions characterized by high friction and wear, where both chemical compatibility and mechanical integrity at the interface are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: A graded or compositional interlayer at the Cu/HEA interface that reduces mismatches in chemical and mechanical properties.
generation.mechanism: The gradual change in composition at the interface enhances chemical compatibility and minimizes thermal/mechanical stress concentrations, thereby securing improved bonding between the Cu substrate and the HEA while maintaining the superior wear resistance of the HEA layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified coating is expected to show significantly improved adhesion to the Cu substrate along with maintained—or possibly enhanced—wear resistance under high-stress service conditions.
generation.baseline: A conventional HEA coating directly applied to a Cu substrate, which typically suffers from poor interfacial adhesion due to chemical and mechanical mismatches.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the graded interfacial layer may be sensitive to the precise composition, thickness, and thermal treatment parameters, thereby limiting the outcome if these factors are not optimized.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in adhesion strength and wear resistance are uncertain without experimental validation; the optimal conditions for the graded layer require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of copper substrates: one with a conventional HEA coating and another with an HEA coating featuring a graded interfacial layer enriched with Cr or Ti. Apply identical deposition and thermal treatment procedures where applicable. Subject both sets to standardized wear testing (e.g., sliding wear tests) and adhesion evaluations (e.g., scratch tests).
measurements: Wear rate and wear depth under controlled sliding conditions
Microscopic analysis of the interfacial microstructure (to confirm the graded composition)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA coating with the graded interfacial layer does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in adhesion strength and wear resistance over the conventional HEA coating on Cu, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. decision.trend: Early work on HEA coatings has focused on developing wear‐resistant, high strength surfaces using advanced processing techniques such as magnetron sputtering and laser cladding. In studies like PMC7304825, nanocrystalline refractory HEA films were successfully deposited and their adhesion improved via post‐deposition annealing on substrates like stainless steel, while PMC10142552 explored compositional modifications (e.g., varying Cr content) to refine microstructure and enhance hardness on steel substrates. However, while these approaches have enhanced the coatings’ intrinsic wear resistance and mechanical properties, they have not directly tackled the challenge of bonding an HEA to a copper matrix.
decision.unsolved: The remaining challenge is to design a coating that not only exhibits excellent wear resistance but also forms a robust, chemically and mechanically sound interface with a copper substrate.
decision.lever: develop a graded interfacial layer—by incorporating adhesion‐promoting elements (such as Cr or Ti) into the HEA composition or as an intermediate layer—deposited via a technique like magnetron sputtering with controlled thermal treatments
decision.why: This step evolves naturally from the trend where post-deposition treatments and compositional tuning improved coating properties. A graded or engineered interfacial layer can specifically address the chemical and mechanical mismatch between copper and the HEA, ensuring strong adhesion while retaining the wear resistance of the bulk HEA coating.
